property_summary: For any nonzero ETH deposit sent to C via its receive() entry, the reference contract always increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant blocks any increase so this property fails for some deposit amounts.

For any payable deposit sent to C via its receive entry, the reference increments depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require prevents any increase, violating this for some deposit amounts.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive() entry, the reference implementation always increases depositsCount by 1; the mutant's added equality check can block that increase for some deposit amounts, violating this rule.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive() entry, the reference C always increases depositsCount by 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can block that increase for some deposits, so there exist inputs where depositsCount does not increase.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract always increments depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can prevent that increase for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any externally-sent nonzero ETH deposit that successfully completes the receive call, the contract's public depositsCount increases by 1; the mutant reverts on receive so some deposits that should succeed leave depositsCount unchanged.

For any externally-sent payable deposit from an EOA, the reference contract's receive() always accepts and increments depositsCount (so depositsCount increases when a deposit is made), whereas the mutant's receive() always reverts and thus does not increment depositsCount for some deposit inputs.

For every payable external caller and nonzero value, calling C's receive() either succeeds and increments depositsCount by 1 (reference) — the mutant makes receive() always revert for some callers/values, violating that for those inputs.

For any external caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C (via an externally-originated payable call), the reference contract's receive() accepts the payment and increments depositsCount by 1; the mutant's receive() always reverts so for some caller/amount the deposit is rejected and depositsCount does not increase.

For any externally-originated successful payable call that transfers nonzero ETH into C, the reference contract's receive() always accepts the payment and increments depositsCount by 1; the mutant's receive() reverts thereby causing such a call to fail (so the property: a successful external payable call to C increases depositsCount by exactly 1 — the mutant makes some such calls fail).

For every call to receive() the contract's depositsCount never decreases (i.e., depositsCount after the call is >= previous depositsCount); the mutant removes the overflow-guarding require so on wraparound inputs the mutant can make depositsCount wrap and violate this rule.

For any deposit amount and sender, calling receive increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (so new depositsCount == old + 1 without silent overflow); the mutant removes the overflow-preventing require and thus can allow a wraparound that violates the monotonic increment rule for some input.

For every deposit call the contract's depositsCount either increments by 1 or the deposit call reverts; the mutant removes the overflow-require and can allow a successful deposit that makes depositsCount wrap (not equal to previous+1) for some input.

For any initial depositsCount and any deposit value, a successful call to receive() on the reference C always leaves depositsCount greater than or equal to its pre-call value (i.e., it never silently wraps to a smaller number); the mutant that replaces the require with require(true) can allow a wraparound on uint overflow making depositsCount smaller than before for some inputs.

For every call to receive funded with any nonzero wei by any sender, the correct contract either reverts (preventing overflow) or leaves depositsCount strictly greater than its previous value; the mutant that replaces the overflow-check with require(true) can allow a successful call that wraps depositsCount to a smaller value for some inputs.

For any nonzero wei sent to C via its receive() by any sender, the contract's public depositsCount never decreases (it is at least its previous value plus 1); the mutant that decrements depositsCount can make depositsCount smaller after a receive call and thus violates this rule for some input.

For any sender and any nonzero wei sent to C via its receive(), depositsCount increases by at least 1 (so c.depositsCount() after receive >= before + 1); the mutant that decrements can make depositsCount smaller for some input.

For any sender and any nonzero wei value sent to C via its receive() the public depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before), but the mutant that decrements can make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some sender/amount.

For any sender and any nonzero wei value sent to C via its receive(), the public depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements depositsCount can make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some fuzzed inputs.

For any sender and any nonzero ether value sent to C via its receive(), the reference implementation always increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that decrements will violate this for some fuzzed sender/amount by making depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1.

After any successful receive() call that sends a positive amount of ETH to the contract, depositsCount strictly increases by 1 (reference preserves monotonic increment); the mutant resets depositsCount to 0 violating this rule for some inputs.

For any payable call to receive that sends a nonzero amount of ether, depositsCount increases (monotonic increment by 1); the mutant resets depositsCount to 0 breaking monotonic increase for some inputs.
On each successful receive() call, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (reference); the mutant increments it by 2 so there exist inputs where depositsCount != previous+1.

For any single payable call to receive, depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant that increments twice can make depositsCount increase by 2 for some input (an ETH amount), violating this invariant.

For any single payable call to receive(), depositsCount increases by at least 1 but no more than 1 (i.e., increases exactly by 1); the mutant that increments twice can make a single receive() increase depositsCount by 2, violating this rule.

For any nonzero ETH sent to C via its receive() by any sender, the reference contract increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount after the receive equals prior+1); the mutant that removed the increment breaks this rule for some input (any positive value).

For any recipient address that reverts on plain transfer (i.e., whose receive()/fallback revert), the reference contract's withdrawAll() uses withdraw(...) which performs a call and thus still results in the contract keeping funds when the external transfer fails (call returns false but does not revert), whereas the mutant that uses payable(msg.sender).transfer(...) will revert and thus withdrawAll() will revert (observable as a different post-call success/failure and leaving contract balance unchanged); hence reference always preserves funds on failing recipient call without reverting the whole transaction, while the mutant does not.

For any callee that reverts on receiving funds, calling withdrawAll() on the correct contract (which delegates to withdraw via low-level call) will NOT revert the withdrawAll call and will leave the contract balance unchanged (the call to the external failing callee is tolerated), whereas the mutant that uses transfer will revert when the callee rejects funds — producing a different success/failure observable outcome for some inputs.

For any recipient that rejects plain transfers, the reference C's withdrawAll does not revert and leaves contract balance unchanged, while the mutant (which uses transfer) will revert — so the reference always returns a successful call (ok = true) for all recipients, whereas the mutant fails for some recipient addresses.

For any recipient address, if withdrawAll() is invoked by the owner after the contract has received some ETH, the reference implementation will always complete (not revert) and thus return ok=true even when the recipient reverts on receiving funds, whereas the mutant using transfer can revert for some recipient behaviors (so ok may be false).

For any recipient behavior and any deposited amount, the reference C's withdrawAll() never reverts (it calls withdraw which uses a low-level call and tolerates a failing external transfer), whereas the mutant using payable(...).transfer(...) can revert for some recipient behaviors (so withdrawAll may revert) — the rule: withdrawAll() returns success (does not revert) for all inputs in the reference, but the mutant fails for some inputs.

Reference contract C always reverts when a non-owner calls an onlyOwner-protected function (observable as withdrawAll reverting / not transferring funds), whereas the mutant silently returns allowing non-owners to call withdrawAll successfully and potentially change contract balance/state.

For any caller/amount where the owner calls withdraw after the contract holds at least that amount, the reference contract always reduces address(c).balance by exactly the withdrawn amount (i.e. succeeds and transfers funds); the mutant using send may fail silently when the recipient's fallback reverts, leaving address(c).balance unchanged, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and amount, when the contract holds at least that amount and the owner calls withdraw(amount) the reference C always reduces address(c).balance by exactly amount (transfer reverts on recipient failure), whereas the mutant using send may silently fail when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts, leaving the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) when the contract currently holds at least amount and the recipient's fallback does NOT revert, C always decreases address(c).balance by exactly amount; the mutant that uses send can silently fail when the recipient's fallback reverts, leaving address(c).balance unchanged for some inputs (thus violating this rule).

For every amount and recipient where the contract has at least that balance and the owner calls withdraw(amount) to send to msg.sender, the reference contract always makes address(c).balance decrease by exactly amount (transfer reverts on recipient failure), while the mutant using send can leave the balance unchanged when the recipient's fallback reverts, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) after the contract holds at least amount and the owner is a regular contract whose fallback reverts, the reference C (using transfer) always causes address(c).balance to decrease by amount (transfer reverts on recipient failure), whereas the mutant (using send and ignoring its false return) can leave address(c).balance unchanged when the recipient's fallback reverts.

For any caller and any withdraw amount, the reference contract always successfully forwards Ether to the owner such that the contract's balance decreases by the withdrawn amount (i.e., withdraw never reverts and reduces address(c).balance by _value); replacing transfer with a low-level call can fail when the recipient's fallback/receive reverts, so the mutant may revert and leave the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For every admissible withdraw amount and recipient behavior, the reference contract's withdraw never reverts when called by the owner (because transfer to the owner either succeeds or reverts consistently for an EOA), but replacing transfer with a low-level call allows the owner transfer to fail when the owner's fallback/revert handler reverts, so the mutant can revert on some inputs (owner being a reverting contract) while the reference does not.

For any withdraw amount and any recipient contract, the reference uses transfer which will always either deliver funds or revert in a way that causes c's balance to decrease by the withdrawn amount when the call returns successfully; replacing transfer with a low-level call can fail (returning false) for a recipient that deliberately reverts on receive(), causing the mutant to revert while the reference would have reverted earlier or behave differently — specifically, there exists a recipient contract behavior (reverting fallback/receive) and a fuzzed withdraw amount such that the mutant's withdraw reverts (ok==false) while the reference's withdraw does not produce the same observable result (the universal property: for all amounts and recipients, calling withdraw as owner should either succeed and reduce address(c).balance by the amount or revert consistently — the mutant breaks this by allowing a low-level call to return false/revert for some recipient).

For any owner and any withdraw amount that was previously deposited into the contract, calling withdraw as the owner always either (1) succeeds and reduces address(c).balance by exactly the requested amount or (2) reverts; the mutant using low-level call can cause the withdraw to revert for a recipient that deliberately reverts while the original transfer would have reverted earlier or behaved differently — specifically, there exists a recipient contract (the owner) whose fallback/receive reverts causing the mutant's low-level call to fail (observable as a failed withdraw) while the reference's behavior differs, so we assert that when the owner is a reverting contract and enough balance was deposited, withdraw must revert on the mutant but not on the reference (i.e., the reference preserves the invariant that a successful withdraw by owner always reduces address(c).balance by the amount).

For any owner and any positive withdraw amount that was previously deposited, calling withdraw as the owner never reverts when the owner is an EOA and reduces address(c).balance by the withdrawn amount; replacing transfer with a low-level call can fail when the owner is a contract whose receive()/fallback reverts, so there exists a contract-owner and amount where the mutant's withdraw reverts or leaves address(c).balance unchanged while the reference still succeeds — we assert that when the owner is a reverting contract and enough balance exists, withdraw() MUST revert (ok==false) on the mutant but the reference satisfies the general rule for EOAs, so deploying a reverting owner distinguishes them (the test uses a reverting-owner helper deployed by the fuzzer-supplied owner address as parameter).

Only the owner can withdraw funds: for any caller and any withdraw amount, after funding the contract the correct contract C preserves that only the deployer (owner) can reduce contract balance via withdraw, whereas the mutant allowing anyone to call withdraw can make the contract balance decrease when a non-owner calls withdraw.

For any target and amount, the reference contract never reverts when sending Ether to a target that may revert (it never forces failure of sendMoney), because it uses low-level call that ignores success; replacing that with transfer causes sendMoney to revert for targets that reject Ether — the mutant thus can revert while the reference never does.

For any target and amount, the reference contract's sendMoney never reverts when the callee rejects or reverts (it performs a low-level call and ignores the return); replacing that with transfer can make sendMoney revert for some targets that reject Ether—so the property: sendMoney always returns (does not revert) for every admissible target/amount in the reference, which the mutant violates for revert-rejecting targets.

For any target address and value, calling sendMoney with a callee whose fallback may revert must never change contract C's balance in the reference (the reference never reverts callers when the callee fails), whereas the mutant which requires the callee call to succeed will revert for failing callees and thus the observable success/failure differs for some inputs.

For any target and value, calling sendMoney on the reference C does not change depositsCount (it only forwards funds); the mutant increments depositsCount after the external call, so for some adversarial target (one that accepts the call) depositsCount will increase in the mutant but remain unchanged in the reference.

For any target address and amount sent by the owner, calling sendMoney forwards that amount out of the contract (reducing address(c).balance by _value); the mutant that removes the external call fails to forward funds for some inputs.

For all callers and amounts, only the contract owner can change C's balance via sendMoney; the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows non-owners to change the contract balance via sendMoney for some inputs.
